articles.title: Tampa Bay comes back in the 12th inning to extend the World Series, holding off Brewers’ championship dreams
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays won Game 4 of the World Series in dramatic fashion, scoring two runs in the bottom of the 12th inning to beat the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body:
Tampa Bay comes back in the 12th to win! The Tampa Bay Rays scored two in the bottom of the 12th inning to overcome a one-run deficit, defeating the Milwaukee Brewers, 4-3, in Game 4. The best-of-seven World Series is now 3-1 in favor of the Brewers.

Extra-inning drama: Cooper Pratt put the Brewers up a run in the 12th inning with a home run, but the Rays answered back in the bottom of the inning with their own rally. Ben Williamson’s pinch-hit single scored Nick Fortes for the winning run.

Tampa Bay faces long odds : Twenty-five previous teams have gone down 0-3 in a World Series. None of them have come back to win.

Game 5 is Wednesday night: The Brewers will have another chance to clinch the title when Game 5 takes place at 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday.

Our live coverage of Game 4 of the 2026 World Series has ended. Find a full recap here and analysis from CNN Sports’ Hannah Keyser here . Our live coverage of Game 5 launches at 7 p.m. ET on Wednesday.

The Tampa Bay Rays gave the Milwaukee Brewers a dose of their own medicine in Game 4 to avoid getting swept Tuesday night (and Wednesday morning) in St. Petersburg, Florida.

The Rays extended their season at least one more day thanks to a walk-off single from Ben Williamson to win the game, 4-3, in 12 innings.

The Rays jumped out to an early lead with an RBI double from Chandler Simpson to get the scoring started in the second inning.

But just as they have all season, the Brewers always seemed to have an answer. Milwaukee leveled the game at 1-1 in the top of the fourth inning on a Cooper Pratt double.

The Rays immediately reclaimed the lead in the bottom of the fourth thanks to a throwing error from Brewers third baseman David Hamilton, who immediately atoned with a game-tying home run in the fifth inning to knot the game at 2-2.

The game would grind on tied 2-2 into the late innings, and eventually into extra innings. As each team exhausted their bullpen and bench, it became a question of which team was going to blink first.

Tuesday turned into Wednesday as the game reached a climactic 12th inning. Pratt struck again for Milwaukee with a towering home run into the left field seats off Tampa Bay reliever Ian Seymour that had the Brewers sitting on the brink of their first championship in franchise history.

But the Rays channeled their inner Brewer in the bottom of the 12th inning. That meant small ball and a lot of traffic on the base paths.

Junior Caminero led off the inning with a bouncer to third base and reached safely on a throwing error by Rays replacement third baseman Joey Ortiz. Liam Hicks followed that with a soft chopper that found its way into left field and moved Caminero to third base.

Next up, Jonny DeLuca hit a seeing-eye grounder back up the middle and through to center field to drive in pinch-runner Cedric Mullins. After failing to get a sacrifice bunt down, Simpson lined a single into center field to load the bases with no one out.

Ben Williamson then stepped to the plate a hit a high chopper over the first baseman’s head and into right field to score pinch-runner Nick Fortes with the game-winning run.

The late game heroics make for a Game 5 on Wednesday where the Rays will once again try to cobble together a win, having used their scheduled Game 5 starter Nick Martinez in relief on Tuesday.

The Brewers will send presumptive National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski to the mound to try to clinch their first-ever World Series title.

Baseball history is long. Basically everything has happened at least once. Except, that is, a comeback in the World Series for a team down three games to zero.

Of the first 25 teams that have ever fallen into such a Fall Classic hole, none came all the way back to win it all. None forced a Game 7. None forced a Game 6. Only four avoided the sweep to even play a Game 5.

The Rays, the 26th such team to find themselves on the ignominious end of a 3-0 start to the World Series, at least have done that much.

They lost each of the first two games in Milwaukee with the tying run standing on third base for the final out. They returned to Tampa, where they enjoyed the AL’s best home record in the regular season, to find Tropicana Field overrun with Milwaukee fans and got embarrassed in a blowout.

At that point, history said they should probably just pack it in.

Instead they battled for 12 innings to keep their season alive and in the end won with a barrage of singles that culminated with the last man off the bench pinch-hitting for a game-winning RBI.

“We got a lot of fight in us,” Chandler Simpson, who has flashed his vastly improved outfield defense through the series while running rampant on the basepaths, said on the Fox broadcast after the game.

The Brewers – the best team in baseball the past two regular seasons – are fantastic, but a sweep would have obfuscated just how close a matchup this series could, and should, be – and was for at least one night (and into the wee hours of the next morning). Tampa is still on the brink.

On Wednesday, though, they get to try to do something no team has ever done before.

And this World Series will continue for another night!

The Tampa Bay Rays battled back in the bottom of the 12th to complete the comeback and win Game 4 of the World Series, 4-3!

It started with an error that allowed Junior Caminero to reach first base, but seemed to cost the team their star on the base paths with an apparent injury. Caminero made it to third base on a single by Liam Hicks, where he was replaced by Cedric Mullins as a pinch runner.

Jonny DeLuca singled to tie it. Chandler Simpson singled to load the bases again.

And then came Ben Williamson, pinch hitting, who singled with a high, looping chopper to drive in the winning run.

Hicks, DeLuca, and Simpson all recorded their hits after getting two strikes. It was, in other words, a rally that looked a lot like what the Brewers have done to the Rays all series and especially in the blow-out fifth inning in Game 3.

Williamson, who got the winning hit, had been 1-for-15 in the postseason before that at bat.

Junior Caminero reached on an error after getting jammed and Liam Hicks’ single moved him over to third base and the tying run is just 90 feet away.

Caminero has been taken out of the game in favor of pinch runner Cedric Mullins, looking to get the tying run across and keep this game going.

Jonny DeLuca blasts a single back up the middle and drives in Mullins! The game is once again tied!

Ian Seymour worked his way through the rest of the 12th inning with no further damage.

There was a bit of history made in the meantime as Brewers left fielder Jackson Chourio collected his second hit of the night and 10th hit of the series with a double into the right-center field gap.

Chourio’s 10 hits through four World Series games ties a record set by Babe Ruth in 1928.

Who’s gonna blink first in St. Petersburg? It didn’t take long to get an answer.

Cooper Pratt collected his fourth hit of the game, and the biggest hit of his career, with a towering homer to left-center off Rays pitcher Ian Seymour.

After Yandy Díaz works a walk, the Rays opt to compromise future innings for the chance to end it in the 12th by replacing him with pinch runner Jorge Mateo.

Mateo does his part and steals second, putting the go-ahead run that would save the Rays’ season into scoring position. But (alas, for all our sleep schedules) that’s as far as he makes it.

Jonathan Aranda flies out and the game continues into the 12th.

Tyler Wells took to the hill again for Tampa Bay as the 11th inning got underway, and he quickly retired Christian Yelich and William Contreras.

Manager Kevin Cash then made the call to the bullpen for Cam Booser, who had a disastrous appearance yesterday in Game 3.

Booser promptly walked Brice Turang on four pitches to bring up Sal Frelick, who has had a few clutch plays in this World Series. Booser was able rebound, though, and retired Frelick with a check-swing strikeout.

The Rays come to the plate with a chance to win Game 4 – again.

Aaron Ashby is back in for the 10th. (Using closer Trevor Megill for just one batter was A Choice, but because it’s the 2026 Brewers, it probably won’t backfire!)

He gets Jonny DeLuca to ground out quickly, makes a slick fielding play and fires a bullet to first to get Chandler Simpson, and strikes out Victor Mesa, Jr., who has five strikeouts in 13 plate appearances this series.

With the exception of the Game 3 blowout, every game in this series has been a nail-biter, and tonight is no exception.

With zero margin for error, the Rays turn to reliever Tyler Wells in the 10th inning.

After a lazy flyout from Joey Ortiz, Jackson Chourio stepped to the plate with visions of a World Series MVP award dancing in his head. Chourio squared one up, but it was a line drive straight at center fielder Jonny DeLuca, who barely had to move to make the catch.

A swinging strikeout of Jake Bauers sends Game 4 to the bottom of the 10th.

Aaron Ashby, who entered the ninth inning working on a historic scoreless streak this postseason, quickly ties Andrew Miller’s record of 16 innings without surrendering a run in October with a strikeout of Jonathan Aranda.

He gets Junior Caminero to ground out – with a help in the at bat from William Contreras’ impeccable pitch challenging – to set a new record. One more ground out by Liam Hicks and we are headed to extras!

Either the Rays’ season will end in heartbreakingly close fashion or they’ll stay alive in a walk-off.

Rays closer Bryan Baker was back on the bump for the ninth inning.

After quickly retiring Sal Frelick, Cooper Pratt collected his third hit of the game with a seeing-eye grounder into left field.

Garrett Mitchell gave the Rays’ faithful a scare with a fly ball to deep left, but Chandler Simpson was there to make a leaping catch at the wall.

On a pivotal play, Pratt tried to swipe second base and put himself in scoring position. Pratt was initially called safe, but the play was challenged by the Rays, and after a lengthy replay review, the call was overturned thanks to a great throw from catcher Liam Hicks and an even better tag from second baseman Richie Palacios.

For just the second time this October, a Rays batter challenged a called strike and it worked! He won! It flipped the count from 2-2 to a hitter favorable 3-1…

And then two pitches later he lined out.

The Brewers call on closer Trevor MeGill to get the final out of the frame and he does. Successful challenge aside, the Rays go down in order and we’re headed to the ninth tied.

With Game 4 (and the Rays’ season) hanging in the balance, Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash made the call to the bullpen for his star closer Bryan Baker in the eighth inning.

Baker doesn’t usually pitch for more than a single inning, but after a breezy eight-pitch inning, the big right-hander will likely be back out again in the ninth inning.

The tension is rising as Tampa heads to the plate with another chance to save its season.

Chandler Simpson’s speed keeps the Rays from going down quietly in the bottom of the seventh.

D.L. Hall comes in to pitch for Milwaukee and gets two quick outs. But then Simpson singles on a ground ball that shortstop Cooper Pratt holds on to rather than risk sowing more chaos by trying to beat Simpson with a throw.

The American League stolen base leader draws a pair of pickoff attempts – which should have given him the chance to run freely as the next one would be a balk – but before gets the chance, Victor Mesa, Jr. grounds out to end the inning.

We’re headed to the eighth in a tied game with a championship on the line.

Nick Martinez was back on the mound for the Rays in the seventh inning, with Fox Sports’ commentators speculating that manager Kevin Cash probably hopes to go with the Game 1 starter the rest of the way tonight.

Martinez appears up to the task with a 1-2-3 inning to send Game 4 to the seventh inning stretch.

Both these teams are good. One is probably better. But also, sometimes, the ball bounces your way and sometimes, well, you get doubled off when you desperately need a rally.

Yandy Díaz slaps a soft single to lead off the inning. And then Jonathan Aranda smacks a ball 108.1 mph off the bat. It had an expected batting average of .890.In other words, nearly nine out of ten times a ball hit just like that ball was hit would have cruised into the outfield and the Rays would have two on with no outs.

Instead, Brice Turang, a Gold and Platinum Glove award winner, swiped the ball out of the air and doubled Díaz off at first. Bases empty, two outs. Next batter, Junior Caminero, grounds out to Turang for good measure and to end the inning.

Desperate times call for desperate measures. Enter Nick Martinez – the Rays’ scheduled Game 5 starting pitcher.

After a strong outing as the starter in Game 1, Martinez looked up to the pressure of the moment in his first inning of relief, retiring the Brewers in a scoreless sixth inning marred only by a bloop single from Cooper Pratt.

As for tomorrow? The Rays will cross that bridge when (if?) they come to it.

It’s an annual tradition that means a lot to many – the Game 4 moment in which players and fans of both teams unite, along with nearly everyone else in the stadium, to remember those lost to cancer.

The pause in the game is powerful and provides a soft moment to remember all those affected by such a terrible disease.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “I didn’t want my children to be like me.” - How Mike Tyson turned the heartbreak of losing daughter into a father’s redemption and enduring legacy
articles.summary: Mike Tyson’s life has been shaped by boxing victories, personal struggles and the loss of his four-year-old daughter, Exodus, in 2009.
articles.body: Mike Tyson’s life has been shaped by boxing victories, personal struggles and the loss of his four-year-old daughter, Exodus, in 2009. The former heavyweight champion has also spoken openly about how fatherhood changed his outlook on life. Although the world remembers Tyson for his power inside the ring, his experiences as a parent offer another side of his story. From growing up in Brooklyn to raising seven children, his journey shows how a difficult past can shape a person’s hopes for the next generation.How did Mike Tyson’s childhood in Brownsville shape himMike Tyson grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, where he faced bullying and trouble at a young age. His father was largely absent from his life, and his childhood brought experiences that later influenced his behaviour and his boxing career.Tyson found direction through boxing after meeting trainer Cus D’Amato. D’Amato became a major influence on the young fighter, helping him develop the skills and discipline that took him to the top of the sport.In 1986, Tyson became the youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history at 20. His speed, power and aggressive style made him one of the most feared fighters of his era. But success in the ring did not mean that the difficulties in his personal life had disappeared.Tyson later spoke about the challenges he faced while growing up and the personal changes he needed to make. His story is not simply about a young man escaping poverty through sport. It is also about the difference between learning to fight opponents and learning to handle life away from the ring.How did the death of Exodus Tyson change Mike TysonOne of the hardest moments in Tyson’s life came in May 2009, when his daughter Exodus died following an accident involving a treadmill cord at her home in Phoenix, Arizona. She was four years old.Tyson was in Las Vegas when he learned about the accident and travelled to Phoenix. The loss was a personal tragedy that no sporting achievement could ease. In an interview on The Oprah Winfrey Show, reported by the Associated Press on October 12, 2009, Tyson called Exodus “my angel.”He also spoke about his family’s importance to him, saying his children were “the only thing that matters to me now.” CBS NewsThe tragedy also brought Tyson’s struggle with grief into public view. In a 2010 interview with CNN’s Larry King, he described the loss as a moment that forced him to grow up and wake up. When asked whether he would ever get over it, Tyson admitted he did not know.His words showed that grief was not something he could simply put behind him. He had to keep living while finding a way to deal with the loss. The death of Exodus remains an important part of his family story, but it should not be reduced to a simple tale of personal redemption.Why did Mike Tyson want his children to have different lives?Tyson’s experience in boxing gave him a clear view of the physical and mental demands of the sport. He knew what it meant to train under pressure, absorb punishment and live with the expectation of winning. He did not want his children to feel they had to follow the same path to make him proud.During an appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, Tyson discussed the freedom he wanted his children to have. Speaking about the pressure parents can place on young athletes, he explained that he did not want his children to feel they had to become the best at everything.His family includes children with different interests and ambitions. Amir Tyson studied broadcast journalism at American University and later built a career in media and business. Miguel Tyson has explored photography and filmmaking, while Morocco Tyson has shown an interest in sports.Their lives have not followed one shared plan. That is an important part of the story: allowing children to choose their own direction does not mean they must all avoid sports or follow a particular idea of success.How are Amir Tyson and Miguel Tyson building their own pathsAmir Tyson’s education and work in media gave him a route outside his father’s original career. He graduated with a degree in broadcast journalism in 2019 and later launched the clothing brand Debonair. He has also worked in boxing commentary, showing that he can build a career around sport without simply copying his father’s achievements.However, Amir’s story has taken a new turn. In September 2026, he officially signed a multi-fight deal with Misfits Boxing. While his professional debut was initially targeted for December, the bout was postponed to February 2027 following the sudden passing of his trainer. Despite the delay, his decision to enter the ring means the idea that all of Tyson’s sons have stayed away from fighting is no longer accurate.Miguel, meanwhile, has explored creative work, including photography and filmmaking. His interests offer another example of how the children have developed their own identities beyond their father’s fame.For Tyson, fatherhood has also meant living with the consequences of his own choices. His past includes serious personal struggles, and his public story has never been free of controversy. Becoming a parent did not erase those experiences, but it gave him another responsibility: supporting his children as they make decisions for themselves.That is what makes his family life more complicated, and more human, than a simple story about a famous fighter raising gentle sons. His children have their own goals, and their decisions will not always match his wishes.What makes Mike Tyson’s story as a father meaningfulTyson’s career brought him fame at an age when most people are still finding their place in the world. His childhood, rise to heavyweight champion and later personal struggles have all been documented. Yet his experiences as a father reveal a different part of his life.The death of Exodus showed the limits of fame and physical strength in the face of a personal loss. His comments about his children also show that he values their ability to make their own choices rather than living under the pressure of his reputation.His family life is not a perfect story, and there is no need to present it that way. Amir’s decision to enter boxing shows that Tyson’s children are free to choose paths that may differ from what their father once imagined for them.What matters is the opportunity to make those decisions for themselves. Tyson’s story offers a reminder that a parent’s legacy is not measured only by trophies, titles or money. It can also be seen in the space children are given to build lives of their own.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Where does Utah rank in some of Morgan Scalley’s key stats for success?
articles.summary: With Utah sitting atop the Big 12 Conference at 7-0, let’s take a look at where the Utes rank in some of Morgan Scalley’s key stats.
articles.body:
Each week, Utah coach Morgan Scalley and his staff pore over film to prepare the team for the opposing team's tendencies and to try to find any weaknesses that the Utes can exploit.

While watching Houston's film, Utah noticed that Houston allowed a lot of quarterback running lanes. Quarterback Devon Dampier was able to use that to his advantage, rushing for 150 yards and two touchdowns in the Utes' 21-13 win over the Cougars.

"We always take what the defense gives us," Dampier said. "Just watching film, there was a lot of running lanes, quarterback lanes during dropback passes. (Coaches) just emphasized, 'Devon, if you see it, go take it.'"

The eye test and film breakdowns are king in football, but statistics and analytics have their place as well, especially as predictors of future success.

Scalley has studied the best teams in college football over the past 20 years and has identified statistics that are indicative of success.

Obviously, scoring offense and defense are the two most important statistics, but digging deeper, what are others that lead to wins?

Rush defense, Scalley says, is a big one. While total rushing yards "doesn't show up as a big stat" for the current top teams in the country, yards per rush is a big tell.

"Are you rushing the ball efficiently? Same thing, passing the ball. Are you passing the ball efficiently? Passing yards, that will never show up. I mean, it rarely shows up in your top programs," Scalley said.

Other telling stats that Scalley looks at include turnover margin and punt return yards.

In his studies, a good amount of the stats most predictive to team success over the past 20 years are on the defensive side of the ball.

"It's why playing great defense is so huge and protecting the football. Chunk yardage plays shows up quite a bit," Scalley said.

With Utah sitting atop the Big 12 Conference at 7-0 and one of just three undefeated teams left in college football, let's take a look at where the Utes rank in some of the stats Scalley mentioned.

Scoring offense: 37.4 points per game (No. 14 in the nation)

The Utes' offense has been potent, especially to start the season. Utah ranks No. 2 in the Big 12 in points per game, but when filtering to just conference games, that number dips from 37.4 points to 30 points, which ranks fifth in the 16-team Big 12.

After scoring at least 31 points in their first five games, Utah has seen a bit of a dip in the last two, scoring 27 points in a win over Colorado and 21 in the victory against Houston.

Scoring defense: 14.6 points per game (No. 9)

Despite allowing more passing yards — 224.1, No. 91 in the nation — than we've come to expect from a typical Utah defense, it hasn't impacted the number that actually matters — opposing points per game.

Utah's defense ranks as one of the best in the country, holding opponents to just 14.6 points per game. In conference play, Utah is allowing 19.5, but still hasn't allowed more than 24 points in any Big 12 game this season.

The standout defensive performance by the Utes came last weekend as Utah held Houston to just 13 points — 26 points below their season average.

The biggest reason why the Utes have kept their opponents' scores low has been a stingy red zone defense. Opponents are scoring in the red zone just 70.6% of the time, 10th-best in the nation, and scoring touchdowns just 47% of the time inside the 20-yard line.

Yards per rush: 5.65 (No. 10); Yards per rush allowed: 3.2 (No. 22)

When Utah runs the ball, it is getting 5.65 yards per rush, good for No. 10 in the nation. Only Big 12 foes Cincinnati — the Utes' next opponent — and Kansas State are averaging more yards per rush.

Wayshawn Parker has been one of the best running backs in the nation and is averaging 6.3 yards per carry, even though teams have keyed in on him as of late. Dampier also contributes to that statistic with 4.7 yards per rush, an impressive showing considering sacks count against quarterback rushing yards in college football.

The Utes have faced some good rushing attacks, like Houston, and have largely shut them down. Utah has been one of the best teams against the rush and have made teams one-dimensional.

Passing efficiency: 158.09 (No. 25); Defensive pass efficiency: 104.24 (No. 6)

The NCAA uses this formula to calculate team passing efficiency, per sports-reference.com : 8.4 * Yds + 330 * TD - 200 * Int + 100 * Cmp) / Att.

Utah, led by Dampier, is No. 25 in the country with a passing efficiency rating of 158.09. That rating is despite six interceptions thrown by Dampier, tied for the most of any team ranked in the top 25 in passing efficiency.

Meanwhile, the defense has been effective in forcing incompletions and holding opposing quarterbacks well below their average completion percentage.

Utah has thrown six interceptions and lost two fumbles, but still has a plus-three turnover margin on the year. The Utes have lived up to the "ballhawks" in Scalley's RSNB initialism, snagging eight interceptions and recovering three fumbles, including a huge one last week that was forced by a Jackson Bennee sack and recovered by Jireh Moe.

Scalley did caution that Dampier has to cut down the interceptions.

"We can't turn the ball over. There's them taking the ball away and then there's us turning it over just with bad decision making and we've had a couple of those," Scalley said.

Punt return yards: 6.67 per return (No. 99); Opposing punt return yards: -0.25 (No. 2)

Utah punt returner Mana Carvalho, who returned a punt for a touchdown last year against Cincinnati, hasn't broken a big one yet, and has had a couple of close calls fielding the ball.

The Utes are averaging just 6.67 yards per punt return, which ranks near the bottom of the FBS.

On the flip side, Utah is No. 2 in the country in punt return defense, holding opponents to -0.25 yards per punt return. Opposing teams haven't had many chances to return the ball, either, with just four returns on the season.

Chunk plays: 77 (No. 8); Opposing chunk plays: 40 (No. 20)

Defining chunk plays as passes of 20 or more yards and runs of 10 or more yards, Utah is tied for No. 8 in the country with 77. The Utes have 51 rushes of 10 or more yards and 26 passes of 20 or more yards.

On defense, Utah is limiting long rushing plays (there have been just 19 rushes of 10 or more yards against the Utes), but have allowed 21 passes of 20 or more yards.

articles.title: Carter Hart injury update: Golden Knights goalie out after leaving morning skate
articles.summary: Vegas' Carter Hart suffered what seemed to be a lower body injury during the morning skate. He was later ruled out for Oct. 27's game.
articles.body:
Vegas Golden Knights goalie Carter Hart was ruled out for Oct. 27's game against the Ottawa Senators , with the goalie exiting during the morning skate on Tuesday.

Hart, who seemingly suffered a lower body injury, appeared to have a limp, per The Hockey News' Hannah Kirkell.

Vegas coach Ryan Craig confirmed Hart would miss the Golden Knights' home game and Adin Hill would start in his place. Hart has a 2.76 goals against average in this fledgling season and an .889 save percentage.

Craig would not provide further updates.

Hart exited the morning skate on Oct. 27 with what appeared to be a lower body injury, as he moved with a noticeable limp.

It is unknown what the extent of Hart's injury is.

Hill has played five games this season, posting a 2.96 goals against average and a save percentage of .882.

The Golden Knights are 4-1 in his starts.

articles.title: Spurs bring designer streetwear, cowboy flair to Frost Bank Center ahead of Kings game
articles.summary: Stephon Castle, Dylan Harper, Devin Vassell and Keldon Johnson showed off their game-day fashion ahead of Tuesday's matchup against the Sacramento Kings.
articles.body:
The San Antonio Spurs brought a mix of luxury streetwear, bold graphics and Texas cowboy flair to Frost Bank Center on Tuesday ahead of their matchup against the Sacramento Kings.

Stephon Castle, Dylan Harper, Devin Vassell and Keldon Johnson showed off their personal styles as they arrived at the arena. Designer labels including Balenciaga, Chrome Hearts, Carhartt WIP and ERCOLE STUDIO made appearances.

The Slash Bros arrived together, with the young Spurs teammates sporting contrasting streetwear looks.

Castle made a statement in a bright red Balenciaga hoodie featuring the fashion house's logo across the chest. He paired it with Balenciaga VIC Skater Graffiti sweatpants, which had an oversized fit and black-and-white, graffiti-inspired graphics. He completed the look with a black-and-white Chrome Hearts Skully Cross Logo beanie and a black backpack.

Harper kept things simple alongside Castle, wearing a black Nike Kobe Bryant hoodie with a small gold Mamba logo on the chest. The Spurs rookie completed his laid-back look with black pants and white sneakers.

Vassell opted for a graphic-heavy streetwear look, wearing an ERCOLE STUDIO gray graphic-print raw-edge T-shirt. The blue-gray shirt featured a woman's face and a lighthouse, with "Holy Water" printed across the front. He paired it with loose-fitting black pants and gray sneakers and carried blue over-ear headphones.

Johnson, meanwhile, brought a little Texas swagger to the arena in a black cowboy hat and a red, black and white Carhartt WIP plaid patch-pocket shirt layered over a black T-shirt. He paired the Western-inspired outfit with black pants and a silver cross necklace. His mustache added another touch of cowboy flair.

From Castle and Harper's coordinated arrival to Johnson's Western-inspired outfit, the Spurs continued to showcase their individual personalities through their game-day fashion.

San Antonio hosts Sacramento on Tuesday night at Frost Bank Center. Tipoff is scheduled for 7 p.m.

articles.title: Hellebuyck Returns Ready To Play For New Jersey Against Dallas
articles.summary: Connor Hellebuyck skips the waiting game, declaring himself ready for Tuesday's debut with New Jersey despite a long suspension and trade standoff.
articles.body:
Connor Hellebuyck is not waiting for permission to start playing again. The veteran goaltender told reporters on Monday that he feels ready to go right now, even though he has not played a game this season. His first appearance in New Jersey comes Tuesday night versus the Dallas Stars, occurring merely four days after a trade from Winnipeg concluded a months-long standoff.

Many athletes let their skills fade when they are stuck on the sidelines, but Hellebuyck did not take that route. ESPN reports that he practiced five to six days weekly in Michigan while suspended. Robby Fabbri and Antonio Stranges, both free agent forwards, trained with him, and he approached these sessions with the same intensity as a full NHL camp. He noted that the goalposts were not drilled into the ice like they are for real games, and both forwards shot left-handed, which limited his practice options. Yet he kept working. He said, "If you're asking me, I'm ready today," Hellebuyck said Monday. "But I don't make every decision around here."

The trade that brought him to New Jersey cost the Devils a significant package. The team sent forward Dawson Mercer, goaltender Nico Daws, prospect Alexander Command, and two draft picks to Winnipeg. This move marks the biggest play yet for first-year general manager Sunny Mehta. Mehta was hired this summer after working with the Florida Panthers. The Devils currently sit at 7-4-0 and are riding a three-game win streak into this road trip.

After spending 11 years with the Winnipeg Jets, Hellebuyck knows the league well, but he still has work to do on his timing. Winnipeg signed him in 2023 to a seven-year contract, and he is currently in the third year of that deal. During that time, he forfeited more than $900,000 in salary because he did not report to training camp. Now he must relearn how to handle screens and rebounds in a new system. "The important part is seeing some screens and reacting to some rebounds, and getting a feel for some righties," said Hellebuyck.

His last start came on April 13 against the Vegas Golden Knights, where he allowed six goals on 38 shots. The Dallas Stars head into Tuesday after winning their last five games. Hellebuyck has a mixed history against Dallas, holding a 14-12-6 record in 32 career meetings. However, his last seven matchups with the Stars have been rough, with just one win and a 3.20 goals-against average. Despite these stats, the mood is positive. "I'm just really excited to play hockey again," Hellebuyck said. "That was the hardest part about all of this, wanting to go back and not being able to."

New Jersey has only one other goalie on the roster, veteran Jake Allen. This means Hellebuyck's arrival immediately changes the team's dynamic. The three-time Vezina Trophy winner and Olympic gold medalist brings a proven track record to a young squad. He finished his tenure with the Jets with a 345-208-55 record over 625 games. That franchise's record in nearly every major goaltending category, such as wins and shutouts, is led by him. The team now faces a tough test against a red-hot Dallas club that looks to extend their winning streak to six games.

articles.title: 49ers star ‘tracking well’ to return after bye week
articles.summary: San Francisco 49ers GM John Lynch likes one of his star's chances to return after the bye week.
articles.body:
Nick Bosa's long wait to return appears to be nearing its end.

49ers general manager John Lynch said Tuesday on KNBR that the star edge rusher is "tracking well" to be back after San Francisco's bye week. Bosa has missed the last five games, dating to Week 3, with a calf injury.

Lynch explained how the team landed on holding him out through the bye despite hope he could return as early as Week 6, and added that that decision wasn't because of an injury setback.

"Bosa had a calf strain, and those are tough. It's another one where you don't want any tightness and soreness, because a reinjury keeps you out even longer," Lynch said. "Kyle was very forthright. Nick was feeling very good. He had pushed it the week prior to the Commanders game and was feeling really good. Then he went out, took it to the next level of where he was actually doing D-line drills, and he got a little sore, and I think that gave everyone pause. That's a signal that it's too soon. I don't think it was a setback. It was just a reality that he wasn't quite there at that point.

The decision was made: let's get him through the bye week. He's got to go through the week of practice, but he's tracking well to be back. Now the goal is to have him back and keep him back, because he's a difference-maker when he's on the field."

Bosa's return is still not locked in, though. He still has to get through a full week of practice, and Lynch's emphasis on keeping him back suggests the 49ers will be careful with a player who got sore the last time he ramped up.

The timing matters for a team that is 6-1 despite the injuries, but fell 29-20 to the Falcons on Sunday. The 49ers return from the bye against the Raiders, and the defensive line would get a major boost if Bosa is back for that game.

articles.title: Did Deion Sanders really offer critics $50,000 to shut up? Here’s the real story
articles.summary: Would Colorado football coach Deion Sanders really pay $50,000 to critics to stop taking about him? No, but he had a point.
articles.body:
Colorado football coach Deion Sanders spent a portion of his weekly news conference Oct. 27 debunking a claim he offered $50,000 to certain people to keep them quiet and stop criticizing him .

"That was a joke," Sanders said Tuesday.

But the claim still caught fire on the internet nonetheless, benefiting from the combustible atmosphere of Sanders' struggles in 2026. His team is 2-5 after five consecutive losses , leading to heightened criticism of Sanders as his team prepares to face Kansas State at home Oct. 31. It marked the latest flash point in a simmering drama between supporters of Sanders and Colorado football fans that have gotten fed up with losing.

Here's how it started and how it's going.

The claim stems from a point Sanders made earlier this year that if he offered some people $25,000 or $50,000 to stop talking, writing and criticizing him and his family for a year, they wouldn't take it because they'd lose money.

"Let's see how that works" Sanders said on Thee Pregame Show in May .

He didn't frame it as a serious offer. He was making a point. There are content creators and news media dedicated to covering what he says and trying to stir the pot about him.

How did this false claim catch fire recently?

One of Sanders' friends, Christopher Neely, came with Sanders from Jackson State to Colorado, where Neely does a podcast on the team and is known as loyal supporter of Sanders. He is granted access to Sanders and his program in exchange.

As criticism about Sanders shot up after a 57-24 loss at Oklahoma State on Oct. 24, Neely recalled Sanders' previous point about the $50,000. He talked about it during a podcast last weekend .

"The people that attack you wouldn't be making the money they were making if he wasn't here (in Colorado) to attack," Neely said. "Which is why he told some of them, 'Hey man, just let's just do this. I give you $50,000 to not mention my name for a year.' And ain't nobody took the deal yet."

Social media users and bloggers took this literally and ran with it without getting further verification under old journalism standards. But he was referring to Sanders' previous point. Then a reporter asked Sanders about it at his weekly news conference on Tuesday.

What Deion Sanders said about $50,000 'offer' Tuesday

A reporter asked him, "Have you offered money for people not to criticize you?"

Neely, who sits near Sanders at news conferences, then reminded Sanders what he said in May — about how some wouldn't take a hypothetical offer of $50,000 to not talk about it for a year because it would be bad for their business.

"Oh, no, no, no," Sanders said told the reporter who asked him about the money offer. "I think you misinterpreted that."

"I would never offer a man money," Sanders said. "I don't give a damn what you say about me. That was really a joke about someone prospering off of your name and your brand, but they don't like you."

Follow reporter Brent Schrotenboer @Schrotenboer . Email: bschrotenb@usatoday.com

articles.title: 3 things that stood out from Purdue basketball's blowout exhibition loss at UConn
articles.summary: The Boilermakers did not shoot it well, and it led to playing from behind. Here's what we learned in the preseason finale.
articles.body:
HARTFORD, CT — Purdue basketball received the challenge it wanted from UConn in its final exhibition and then some, falling 76-53 at PeoplesBank Arena on Tuesday.

The Boilermakers remained winless in their recent run of exhibition road games against high-major opponents. C.J. Cox scored 18 points, but functional offense was hard to come by for much of the night.

Purdue basketball photos vs. UConn in college basketball action

Purdue couldn't make a 3, couldn't muster enough functional offense elsewhere

Matt Painter wanted to play UConn for the simple reason the Huskies "run good offense and make it hard for you to run good offense." He probably wasn't expecting a 1-for-14 first-half shooting performance from 3, a handful of missed opportunities inside and a generally flat offensive performance. (That one made 3 came when Raleigh Burgess whiffed a layup but got the ball back and found Jack Benter behind the line.)

Purdue does not need to be explosive on offense this season, but it must be efficient. Instead, it looked off-kilter for much of the first half. Between those missed 3s and turnovers it had 18 empty offensive possessions in the first half alone. It finished 2_-25 from 3, which probably won't happen often. The inability to create fast break chances or finish around the rim may actually be bigger concerns.

Purdue received a final rebounding reminder before season's start

UConn projected as a much more significant rebounding challenge, and delivered. Three of the Huskies' offensive rebounds came on one possession which did not yield points, but in general, Purdue had a harder time rewarding itself for stops than in the first two exhibitions. UConn also set a tone with the way it attacked off defensive rebounds, beating the Boilers down the floor for a couple of 3s and a run-out dunk in the first eight minutes of the game.

When Purdue flipped the rebounding advantage in the opening minutes of the second half, it started to cut into the lead. It simply couldn't convert enough on offense to ever challenge to take the lead.

Braylon Mullins back on the floor, again facing off with Luke Ertel

Greenfield-Central alum Braylon Mullins made his exhibition debut for UConn after missing the first two with an unspecified injury. He provided some hints as to his affliction, though, wearing braces on both knees. When he subbed out of the game, he immediately went to a stationary bike positioned near the court. Purdue kept the NCAA Tournament hero in check — seven points on 3-9 shooting — but he also distributed four assists in the first half.

He and Purdue freshman Luke Ertel, a Mt. Vernon grad, went head-to-head in some memorable high school games. He scored two points on 1-4 shooting in this Hancock County reunion.

Nathan Baird and Sam King have the best Purdue sports coverage, and sign up for IndyStar's Boilermakers newsletter .

articles.title: Valkyries stars tells fans to ‘call in sick’ for Game 6 as early WNBA Finals tipoff sparks fan reaction
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries will play Game 6 at 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday
articles.body: Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries has been moved up to 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday to give State Farm Arena enough time to get the building ready for an NBA game that evening. The early tipoff could create a challenge for fans in California, where the game will begin at 9:30 a.m. PT. The Valkyries defeated the Dream in Monday’s Game 5 in San Francisco to take a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven series, meaning Game 6 could determine the WNBA champion. While championship series games, especially potential championship-clinching contests, are routinely played in prime time, Thursday’s less-than-ideal scheduling doesn’t appear likely to stop Valkyries fans from tuning in to watch their favorite team. WNBA FINALS GAME 6, A POTENTIAL TITLE-CLINCHER, WILL BE HELD IN THE AFTERNOON ON THURSDAY Warriors coach Steve Kerr is among those who plan to tune in, even if he’s having breakfast when the game is starting. "We’ll have a day off that day, so, yeah, I’ll be watching," he said. Several of the WNBA Finals games have drawn record ratings, showing how much interest there is in the league, this series and its athletes. The Valkyries have sold out every game since they began as an expansion franchise last year. Shaunice Christmas-Miller and her wife, Kendall, have attended every home playoff game this season at Chase Center. Their jobs allow them to be flexible and work from home Thursday. Nevertheless, the couple believes the fan base will still show up Thursday. "Absolutely, they will definitely find a way," Shaunice said. Valkyries co-owner Peter Guber was largely unconcerned that the franchise’s devoted home crowd would come together when it matters most, despite morning challenges such as commuter traffic heading into San Francisco for a watch party. DREAM COACH KARL SMESKO CALLS WNBA FINALS OFFICIATING ‘JUST RIDICULOUS’ AS ANGEL REESE ALSO QUESTIONS REFS Supporters have been invited to gather outside Chase Center’s Thrive City viewing area beneath the big screen. Shaunice added that she wishes everybody involved had considered the various options well in advance to avoid such last-minute scrambling. "They should have thought ahead for the whole seven-game series," Shaunice noted. "The women deserve primetime slots." Others expressed their feelings on social media. Rapper Flavor Flav posted Tuesday: "Thursday is a paid holiday. Because Flavor Flav said so." Included in his post was a photo of a note directed to bosses everywhere as a permission slip of sorts requesting excused absences for employees, signed by Flavor Flav with dual titles beneath his name — "The World’s Greatest Hype Man" and "Official Supporter of Women’s Sports." Ole Miss women’s coach Yolett McPhee-McCuin sounded off. "I’d rather play anywhere else than have a 12:30 tip for a WNBA FINALS game man! Not a good look! For fans and for the players," she posted on X. "Just my 2cents that no one asked for." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Golden State coach Natalie Nakase and her players have focused all along on what they can control, and this certainly isn’t one of those things. But there were some clever postgame offerings: "Call in sick, I recommend it," point guard Veronica Burton cracked. "Yeah, right? Y’all know how to fake a cough, didn’t we all do that?" teammate Kiah Stokes added. articles.title: Lincoln Riley affirms his commitment to USC with his 5th season teetering on failure
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Southern California is teetering on the edge of another failure in its College Football Playoff quest. Lincoln Riley's coaching tenure doe...
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Southern California is teetering on the edge of another failure in its College Football Playoff quest. Lincoln Riley's coaching tenure doesn't appear to be on much sturdier footing.

Riley says he isn't ready to give up on either one.

Riley affirmed his love for USC and his confidence in his program's direction as he prepares the Trojans (6-2) to face No. 2 Ohio State on Saturday night with their Playoff hopes in precarity.

"My job is to stay steady," Riley said Tuesday at USC's $225 million Bloom Performance Center, which opened this year. "If I didn't want to be at this place, I wouldn't have come here in the first place. If I didn't want to be at this place, I've had plenty of opportunities to leave. This is where I want to be. This is the right place for me. I'm the right person to be here."

Riley acknowledged he understands why questions are being asked about his future after USC's embarrassing 24-7 loss at Wisconsin last weekend in the worst offensive output ever from a Riley-led team. The Trojans are unranked two-thirds of the way through the fifth season of Riley's tenure, during which he has yet to earn a conference title or a Playoff berth.

USC paid top dollar to poach Riley from Oklahoma because it was determined to get out of the mediocre rut in which this once-dominant program had spent the previous decade. Riley hasn't delivered that level of success on the West Coast, but he insists it's still possible this season and in the future.

"I love it here," Riley said. "There's not too many people in college football history that gave up what I gave up to come here, so I don't care if it's 15 years down the line, that never should be taken lightly. I came here because this is where I wanted to be. I came here because I believe in this place, and none of that has changed whatsoever."

Riley, a Texas native who had never coached west of Lubbock before moving to USC, disagrees with the outside notion he hasn't been a good fit in Los Angeles.

He also said his relationship with athletic director Jen Cohen, who replaced Mike Bohn in 2023, is "fantastic. She's a tremendous AD. Even though she's not the AD that I came here with and I'm not the head coach that she hired, (it's a) fantastic relationship. She's been a huge part of the progress that we've made and has been incredibly supportive."

USC chose Riley to replace Clay Helton, the longtime assistant who got the job in bizarre circumstances and held it for a shockingly long time before his firing in 2021 .

But Riley is 41-20 with the Trojans, while Helton was 39-22 at the same point in his widely criticized tenure.

And USC would have to do something extraordinary to earn the school's first Playoff berth over the next four games: Three of the Trojans' final four opponents are currently in the top seven of the AP Top 25, sporting a combined record of 20-2.

After Ohio State and a bye, USC travels to defending national champion Indiana before finishing the regular season against Maryland and No. 7 UCLA. The crosstown Bruins' success this season under first-year coach Bob Chesney is particularly galling to Trojans faithful who see their own dreams being realized in Westwood.

But Riley isn't giving up, and neither are his players.

"I know he's the right guy," left tackle Elijah Paige said. "Coach Riley is actually the reason I came here. I believe there's not a better leader in the country, and I love going to war for Coach Riley. I believe everybody in this locker room and this entire building thinks the same thing."

articles.title: La democratización de la gimnasia
articles.standfirst: Más allá de los cuatro países que acaparan los títulos hay un puñado interesante de otros territorios. Se acaba de estrenar Noruega, Argelia consolida una estrella
articles.summary: Más allá de los cuatro países que acaparan los títulos hay un puñado interesante de otros territorios. Se acaba de estrenar Noruega, Argelia consolida una estrella
articles.body: Se tiene la falsa creencia de que la gimnasia es un deporte monopolizado por cuatro países, pero los recientes acabados Mundiales de Rotterdam, con 16 banderas en el medallero, han recordado que es una mirada demasiado ligera. Lo interesante no está arriba, donde una vez más Estados Unidos y China han encabezado la tabla, a la espera del pleno regreso de Rusia, que aquí lo hizo aún con veto a algunos de sus gimnastas. Japón es el cuarto. Lo sobresaliente es ver a nuevos países como Noruega, que logró la primera medalla de su historia con Sebastian Sponevik, bronce sin entrar en los pronósticos, China Taipei —oro en barra fija— o la consolidación de Armenia, país que como parte de la Unión Soviética tuvo grandes especialistas como Shahinyan, y Argelia. El mapa sin duda se está ensanchando. Argelia no es sólo Kaylia Nemour, una estrella y campeona olímpica, cuyo comportamiento fue elogiable. Llegaba como una de las gimnastas que debía estar en el podio de concurso completo y puso la mejor nota en la calificación. Pero falló en un salto en la final y se quedó sin opciones. Acabó cuarta. En un deporte en el que parece que lo único que importa son esas medallas podía sonar a naufragio, pero se rehizo como sólo se imagina a gente como Simone Biles y ganó dos oros en asimétricas y la barra de equilibrios. Además, esta vez no ha comparecido sola. Su país se metió por primera vez en la prueba por equipos en los Mundiales. Es algo sintomático. Cuando un combinado deja de depender de una sola figura, el resultado deja de ser una anécdota para convertirse en un proyecto. Al calor de una figura, como le ocurrió a Brasil con Rebeca Andrade, pueden aparecer sorprendentes resultados en el futuro. ¿Y España? No corren buenos momentos para un deporte que ha dejado de estar de moda, sustituido por otra corriente más cool. La generación del plinton y posteriores crearon una época dichosa con Jesús Carballo, ahora de presidente, como referencia antes de la llegada de Gervasio Deferr, seguramente el deportista con más talento puro que ha alumbrado este país. La medalla de Ray Zapata en Tokio se antoja el canto del cisne al menos momentáneamente. La rítmica es la locomotora ahora de esa federación y está que se sale.

articles.title: Diagnosed with polio at 7, Neeraj Yadav, 42, won 3 Asian Para Games golds before a doping ban and a life cut short
articles.summary: Neeraj Yadav, one of India's leading para-athletes, was found dead at a flat on Tuesday night, leaving the para-sports community in shock.
articles.body: Neeraj Yadav, one of India's leading para-athletes, was found dead at a flat on Tuesday night, leaving the para-sports community in shock. The 42-year-old, a three-time Asian Para Games gold medallist, allegedly died by suicide. He is suspected to have consumed poison.A postmortem examination was underway at Delhi’s GTB Hospital on Wednesday.Who was Neeraj Yadav?Born on February 10, 1984, Yadav hailed from Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh. He was diagnosed with post-polio residual paralysis at the age of seven after suffering neural damage.Despite the challenges, Yadav continued to pursue his sporting dreams. He played wheelchair tennis for around seven years, from 2005 to 2012, before turning to para-athletics in 2015. His father was a wrestler and a volleyball player. Yadav got married in 2018.His first major success in athletics came at the 2015 Delhi State Athletics Meet. He won gold medals in the shot put, javelin and discus events, marking the beginning of his journey in the sport.Asian record and three gold medalsYadav made his mark internationally at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Indonesia. Competing in the men's F55 javelin throw, he won gold with an Asian-record effort of 29.84 metres.He returned to the top of the podium at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games in 2023, winning gold medals in both the discus and javelin events. His discus gold came in the F54/55/56 class on October 24, while he won the men's F55 javelin title on October 28.The two victories took his Asian Para Games gold medal tally to three.Yadav also won gold at the Para Athletics Grand Prix in Marrakech, Morocco, in September 2022, setting a new Indian national record. Earlier, he had claimed silver medals in the men's F55 shot put and discus events at the Fazza Grand Prix in 2016.Doping caseYadav's career faced a major setback after an anti-doping case in 2023. The National Anti-Doping Agency provisionally suspended him after an out-of-competition sample collected in Bengaluru in October that year tested positive for stanozolol, an anabolic steroid.He later sought DNA testing of his sample through the anti-doping disciplinary process. articles.title: Arsenal knocked out of League Cup by fourth-tier Fleetwood Town
articles.summary: Fourth-tier Fleetwood beat 10-man Arsenal 5-3 on penalties in ⁠the League Cup last 16, pulling off a major upset.
articles.body:
Arsenal suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood Town in a League Cup penalty shootout.

Mikel Arteta’s side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth-round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time on Tuesday.

Arsenal’s Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shootout and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood’s winner.

Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval.

Arsenal’s 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.

Arteta paid the price for prioritising Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.

No one would have predicted Arsenal’s embarrassment regardless of Arteta’s selection gamble.

They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday.

But instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club’s glittering history.

Arsene Wenger’s Arsenal suffered a shock League Cup loss against fourth-tier Bradford on penalties in 2012.

Arteta’s team were beaten by second-tier Southampton in the FA Cup last season and also lost to Nottingham Forest, then in the Championship, in the same competition in 2022.

Supporters of an older vintage will recall Arsenal’s 1969 League Cup final loss against third-tier Swindon and their 1992 FA Cup exit at fourth-tier Wrexham.

But even those painful defeats cannot compare with this remarkable result.

For once, Arsenal fans will not have fond memories of Highbury – Fleetwood’s ground shares the same name as the Gunners’ ancestral home before their move to the Emirates Stadium in 2006.

Fleetwood’s tiny 5,327-capacity ground, where goals are celebrated with a burst of the children’s cartoon song Captain Pugwash over the tannoy, is a far cry from the famous marble halls and dignified grandeur of Arsenal’s former stadium.

Now it will be remembered forever as the site of Arsenal’s most chastening loss in the Arteta era.

Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor wept tears of joy as disbelieving fans flooded the pitch to celebrate their club’s astonishing victory.

Only Myles Lewis-Skelly and Gyokeres kept their places from the Everton game, with teenagers Dowman and Marli Salmon starting, while 18-year-old winger Ceadach O’Neill made his debut.

Languishing in 18th place in League Two, Fleetwood had lost their previous two league games against Exeter City and Cheltenham, yet they showed no signs of being intimidated by their illustrious visitors.

After an eight-minute delay due to an unauthorised drone flying over the stadium, Arsenal were caught cold on a windy night by the Irish Sea.

Fleetwood are nicknamed the “Cod Army” in reference to the town’s fishing industry, so it was somewhat fitting that a mistake from Salmon netted their opener in the 21st minute.

Salmon’s lack of experience was brutally exposed when Loupalo-Bi muscled his way past the 17-year-old with ease, racing into the penalty area to plant a low finish past debutant keeper Illan Meslier.

Arsenal monopolised possession after that shock, but Arteta grew visibly agitated with their lack of cutting edge.

Arteta sent on Martin Odegaard at half-time, and Gyokeres bagged Arsenal’s equaliser five minutes later.

It was a scrappy effort that left Fleetwood feeling aggrieved as Gyokeres wrestled with his marker before poking O’Neill’s ball past Lynch from close range.

Dowman saw red in the 85th minute, dismissed for kicking out at Harrison Neal after a strong challenge from the Fleetwood midfielder.

Although it looked a harsh decision, Arteta was unimpressed with Dowman, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.

Both teams scored their first three penalties in the shootout, but Guimaraes was denied by Lynch and Haughey held his nerve to seal the biggest shock in League Cup history.

articles.title: Beat Luke Littler: Teenagers Jayden Walker and Mitchell Lawrie set to challenge world No 1 to win £501,000
articles.summary: Teenage darts sensations Jayden Walker and Mitchell Lawrie are both hoping to beat world champion Luke Littler; Watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22
articles.body:
Two-time World Youth Championship winner Mitchell Lawrie, 15, and Jayden Walker, 14, will both compete against the World No 1 in Netflix's Beat Luke Littler event on Friday, where the winner will take home an eye-watering bounty of £501,000.

The youngsters are just two of 24 finalists who could face the reigning world champion: if one of the contestants beat Littler, the event will end and they will take home the prize, with Littler having to win 24 legs in a row to deny his opponents.

Both Lawrie and Walker have faced Littler before and are laser-focused on the task at hand, but there is little doubt that there will be plenty more to come from the pair.

"It's life-changing money so I'm looking forward to it," Lawrie told Sky Sports .

"I just obviously hope I get to get the chance to play because I know there are also 24 other good players that have been picked. I'm just hoping to get a chance to play Luke."

Lawrie, a Target Darts ambassador, is the more experienced of the two teenagers, having already surpassed Littler's record to become the youngest player to win a match at the World Darts Federation World Championship, and has even come close to tasting victory against Littler before.

"It was three or four years ago [that I played Luke Littler]. And he beat me 3-2 - I missed a few match darts!

"But that was before he went on to be what he is. And before I went on to be what I was as well."

'I'm 100 per cent expecting to beat Littler'

Lawrie's lofty ambitions do not stop at beating Littler.

The Scot - who turns 16 next week - confirmed to Sky Sports he will be participating in the PDC's Qualifying School in 2027, giving him an opportunity to earn a two-year Tour card and become a regular on the professional circuit.

"No, I'm not thinking about it; I'm definitely doing [the Q-school] - that's what I want to do," he added.

"I've wanted to be a professional darts player since I started. And that's what we're going to try to do in January.

"Hopefully, I'll get my tour card there and then go on to bigger and better things.

"As I've said, I've loved the WDF system and stuff. They've been great with me and I've enjoyed that a lot. But the money's right in the PDC.

"That's where you can make a living out of darts. So, that's where you need to go."

Contestants had to complete 501 in 24 darts or fewer to progress through the first stage of Netflix's auditions, powered by Target OMNI and DartCounter.

Should the Scot get the chance to face Littler once more, he will only have to win one leg, rather than the three he needed last time out - and this time, he has a clear plan of action.

He said: "100 per cent [I'm expecting to beat him].

"It's one leg. He'll be up there throwing. I don't imagine I'll be on close to the start.

"Hopefully I'll win the bull-up and then hit two trebles to start -and then we'll see where the leg takes us. But that's the plan. Win the bull-up, hit two trebles, and then we'll see where it goes from there."

Walker: I've only hit three nine-darters!

While Lawrie is vocally confident in his chances of beating Littler and his prospects as a professional, Walker - a year his junior - is more understated about his astonishing list of teenage darting achievements.

"I've hit quite a few 170s, but I've only hit three nine-darters," Walker told Sky Sports. " The last nine-darter was in February last year.

"I've been so close to hitting double 12 a few times, but hopefully it'll come. You see the professionals on the TV, they probably hit about three or four a week - compared to them, it's not much at all.

"But hopefully, as I develop my game more, I can hopefully hit more and maybe I can get one competitively in a game."

Walker beat world No 2 Luke Humphries when he was only 12 years old, averaging 102 - prompting Humphries to call him "the best 12-year-old [player] I've ever seen in my life" - but is yet to convince his parents that his aspirations of becoming a professional darts player should be his top priority.

"My mum always tells me I have to finish my homework before I can go out to a night of darts. Because I love darts so much, I sort of make myself do the homework.

"[One of my favourite subjects is] maths - it helped me in darts, because during lockdown when I first started playing, I started focusing on it.

"The only schoolwork they set us was maths. I just did maths and all those mental arithmetics helped me with my game, with all the shots out."

Like Lawrie, Walker has faced Littler before - but the Dorset native knows he stands to gain from the profile of the event even if he doesn't get the chance to face the world No 1 for the prize.

"I'm excited for Friday. Obviously, I've been putting in a few hours this morning and I'll probably be putting in a few after this interview and for the rest of the week really, so I know I've got to practise and dedicate myself to beating him.

"I've met Luke before. I've played him twice as well, actually.

"He beat me easily the first time, but then the second time it was quite a competitive game. If I do end up playing him on Friday, hopefully it'll be competitive.

"Even if I don't get to play Luke on the night, it'll be good publicity for being on Netflix. Hopefully I can get a few sponsors that can help me travel on the back of that. And a few followers, that'd be quite nice."

Both Walker and Lawrie will aim to take centre stage and beat Littler to the £501,000 on Friday - and it looks set to be the first of many times darts fans will see the teenage sensations on their screens for years to come.

articles.title: Where does Arsenal’s Fleetwood humiliation place in English cup shocks?
articles.summary: How big a shock is the Premier League champions’ 5-3 defeat on penalties after a 1-1 draw with a fourth-tier club?
articles.body:
Arsenal suffered a stunning League Cup fourth-round defeat at fourth-tier Fleetwood Town on Tuesday.

The Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties after a 1-1 draw in one of the greatest shocks in the history of English football.

The debate over what is the biggest upset in cup history is never-ending, but here are five other epic cup upsets to rival Arsenal’s humiliation.

In the previous season, 90 places had separated the two clubs in the English Football League, with Arsenal having claimed their second title in three seasons under manager George Graham.

Alan Smith put the Gunners in front, but Mickey Thomas’s free kick levelled matters with 10 minutes remaining, and Steve Watkin astonishingly claimed a late winner.

Chelsea won the FA Cup five times between 2006 and 2018, but Jose Mourinho’s Blues were humbled by third-tier Bradford at Stamford Bridge.

The Premier League leaders went 2-0 up through Gary Cahill and Ramires.

But Bradford stormed back, and goals from Jon Stead, Filipe Morais, Andy Halliday and Mark Yeates left Chelsea in tatters .

Hereford beat Newcastle 2-1 (1972 FA Cup)

The fourth-round tie that had everything: pitch invasions by Parka-clad fans, and Ronnie Radford scoring one of the FA Cup’s greatest goals.

Malcolm Macdonald put Newcastle ahead eight minutes from time, and it seemed as if there would be no fairytale for the non-league outfit.

But Radford equalised with a screamer from 25 yards, and Ricky George won it for Hereford in extra time.

Wimbledon beat Liverpool 1-0 (1988 FA Cup final)

Wimbledon’s “Crazy Gang” were given no chance to stop Liverpool from claiming a league and cup double in the final at Wembley.

Wimbledon had been a third-tier side four years earlier, and Liverpool had won the title by a margin of nine points.

But Lawrie Sanchez headed home from Dennis Wise’s free kick, before Wimbledon keeper Dave Beasant saved John Aldridge’s penalty to seal the upset.

Grimsby beat Manchester United 12-11 on penalties (2025 League Cup)

United trailed 2-0 as Grimsby duo Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren scored to expose the flaws in their supposedly superior opponents.

Bryan Mbeumo and Harry Maguire managed to take the second-round tie into extra time.

But Grimsby won on penalties to leave then-United boss Ruben Amorim shell-shocked.

articles.title: Rare Debut Win For Red Wings Homegrown Goalie
articles.summary: The performance by Detroit Red Wings goalie Michal Postava in his first NHL start, as he downed Connor McDavid and […]
articles.body:
The performance by Detroit Red Wings goalie Michal Postava in his first NHL start, as he downed Connor McDavid and the Edmonton Oilers on the road was impressive.

"Postava, we're so excited for him and happy for him," Red Wings coach Todd McLellan told reporters after the game. "Sometimes that's how it happens. A goalie gets a start such as this one and plays really well and gets the win.

YOU ALREADY KNOW🦺 pic.twitter.com/fznL5avMvq — Detroit Red Wings (@DetroitRedWings) October 27, 2026

YOU ALREADY KNOW🦺 pic.twitter.com/fznL5avMvq

Detroit Red Wings (@DetroitRedWings) October 27, 2026

Since 1990, only 12 homegrown goalies have made their NHL debut between the posts for the Red Wings. Postava was just the fifth among that group to earn the win in his first NHL start. He's just the third Detroit goalie to do so since 2005.

The Red Wings have seen a bright future ahead for Postava since they signed him as an undrafted free agent in the summer of 2025. He was stalwart and consistent last season with the AHL Grand Rapids Griffins . Postava took things up another notch in his stinginess so far this season.

When he was called up, Cossa was 4-0 with a 1.25 GAA and .954 save percentage for the Griffins.

"He may be smaller than some of the monsters that are in the league right now, but he is very athletic," McLellan said. "We think that he anticipates so well he can read where the shot release is going. He gets into position, and then there's not a lot that lays around after."

CINEMA pic.twitter.com/2tq9NfFCkl — Detroit Red Wings (@DetroitRedWings) October 27, 2026

In the win, Postava stopped all three shots he faced in the shootout, including the one from NHL scoring leader McDavid.

"Yeah, it's crazy," Postava told reporters. "Like, he's one of the best players that ever played. And I'm just happy now and don't have words."

Red Wings Not Known For Growing Their Own Goalies

Historically, the Red Wings are big spenders when it comes to goalies. They sign UFAs. They trade for high-end talent.

Homegrown puckstoppers are few and far between in Hockeytown. Postava is the first one to make his first NHL start for Detroit since Jared Coreau. On December 3, 2016, Coreau suffered a 5-3 loss to the Pittsburgh Penguins.

Postava is the first Red Wings goalie to win his first NHL start in a Detroit uniform since fellow Czech goalie Petr Mrazek beat the St. Louis Blues 5-1 on February 7, 2013.

Jimmy Howard (Nov. 28, 2005, 5-2 win vs. the Los Angeles Kings), Norm Maracle (March 17, 1996, 4-3 win vs. Edmonton) and Kevin Hodson (January 6, 1996, 3-0 win vs. the Chicago Blackhawks) also were winners when they made their first NHL start for the Red Wings.

Chris Osgood and the Red Wings fell 6-3 to the Toronto Maple Leafs on October 15, 1993, in his first NHL start. Scott King got his first NHL start for the Red Wings on January 28, 1991, against the New Jersey Devils. He didn't figure in the decision as Detroit lost 6-2.

Sebastian Cossa (December 9, 2024 vs. the Buffalo Sabres), Tom McCollum (March 30, 2011 vs. St. Louis), Kaden Fulcher (April 6, 2019 vs. Buffalo), and Dave Gagnon (January 26, 1991 vs. St. Louis) all made their NHL debuts with Detroit in relief appearances. None of them ever started an NHL game for the Red Wings.

Cossa actually got the win against the Sabres in his NHL bow.

articles.title: FIA partners with AWS to help drive future F1 regulations
articles.summary: Motorsport's governing body will use AWS's cloud and AI tools to improve its ability to shape technical regulations
articles.body:
The FIA has announced a wide-ranging partnership with Amazon Web Services as it aims to upgrade its digital capabilities.

AWS will join as its Official AI and Cloud Computing Partner, as the governing body will use AWS's suite of AI tools to improve its capability to produce future technical regulations.

The FIA also runs its aerodynamic simulations on AWS's High Performance Computing technology, allowing it to conduct air flow tests in the virtual world without having to build physical parts, speeding up the process and reducing the costs involved.

This partnership also expands the digital licensing platform the governing body uses to simplify tasks like licence administration, which should make it easier for national sporting authorities to run their events and for officials to sign up. That digital platform, first trialled in Canada and Sri Lanka, will now be rolled out across more countries.

The AWS integration forms part of the FIA's wider digital transformation, as president Mohammed Ben Sulayem explained. "Technology is changing every part of our sport, and the FIA must lead that change. Our new partnership with AWS will support everything from the cars of the future to the grassroots clubs where so many careers begin.

"By bringing world-class cloud and AI technology into the heart of the FIA, we can make it simpler for drivers, officials and volunteers to take part, help our Member Clubs work more efficiently, and move closer to our ambition of doubling global motor sport participation."

AWS is already an existing partner of F1 management, having joined in 2018 as its innovation technology partner. Among other services, AWS tools process telemetry data for broadcast use, powering live strategy predictions.

articles.title: Fennville's mother-daughters combo connects championship volleyball teams
articles.summary: The Winne sisters led Fennville to its first conference volleyball title in 25 years, when their mom was on the team.
articles.body:
Fennville hosts Black River in girls volleyball

FENNVILLE - When Morgan Winne played volleyball for Fennville High School, the team was strong.

The Blackhawks won the SAC conference title in 2000 and 2001, winning a district championship in the latter.

"It started in 2000. We had a really good team and won conference my junior and senior year. We had really good chemistry and won districts in 2001 as well. We want to strive for that this year, too," Winne said. "We have been trying to build that culture back up and we are on an upward trajectory."

That trajectory has been fun for the Winne family as Morgan Winne is an assistant coach with daughters Marynn and Adelynn on the team.

"It has been really fun to see them come out of their shells and just gain confidence throughout the season," Morgan Winne said. "It is really special to have them experience what I did 25 years ago."

The next generation of Winnes understand how special this opportunity is, especially with their mom getting to share in the journey.

"She has been there for me and my sister, supporting us," Marynn said. "Us being together definitely creates a stronger bond."

There are, of course, struggles and challenges with having a mom for a coach - and a sister for a teammate.

"We definitely argue a lot because we are siblings, but that also makes us stronger. We have a strong energy together on the court," Adelynn said. "It is definitely nostalgic for her and she has helped us understand what it takes to get here.

"It is challenging to be a mom and a coach. You feel like you need to be tougher on your own kids. It is hard to separate that boundary and find the balance," Morgan said. "It is very exciting to see all the hard work. We have always known it has been possible and to have them taste what it is like to win, they are understanding their potential. It is really fun to see, especially with my two girls on the team."

The Blackhawks will have all three Winnes together again next year as they look to keep the momentum of the program upswing going.

"It means a lot to us. We knew it was a possibility but we had to work hard and work together to get it," Marynn said. "It definitely gives us a boost for the years to come, knowing what it takes to win conference."

articles.summary: Who are these guys that look to take Notre Dame basketball back toward the top of the ACC standings in 2026-27? Here's more on swingman Ethan Roberts.
articles.body:
We're almost there, almost back to the grind of another Notre Dame basketball season. Before you know it, there will be a foot of snow on the ground, temperatures will be below zero and another Atlantic Coast Conference game will be going up and down the court inside Purcell Pavilion.

To get you ready for those nights and get you ready for a Notre Dame season that starts in Rome on November 1 against Villanova in the Eternal City Tip-off, we'll take a numerical player-by-player look — from 0 to 51 with several stops in between — at the 2026-27 Notre Dame basketball team over the next 16 days (Monday, October 12 thru Friday, October 30).

Who are these guys? What did they do last year? Where do they fit in this one? And what does fourth-year head coach Micah Shrewsberry think of them? Your snapshot of the 2026-27 Irish starts here.

25-26 stats: Averaged a team-high 16.9 points, 3.9 rebounds and 2.3 steals in 30.4 minutes over 23 games, all starts, for a Penn team that finished 18-12, won the Ivy League and went to the NCAA Tournament. Roberts shot .401 percent from the field, .404 from 3 and .799 from the foul line.

26-27 outlook: Bring toughness, experience and scoring to the wing guard spot, where he should be a starter from Day One. Roberts is a known scorer, but also brings a certain don't-back-down-mentality that might be most needed for this program.

Shrews on Roberts: "If you've never watched him and you watch him walk out on the court, (you think) he's a shooter. Ethan's a scorer. He'd rather drive than shoot. The 5-foot-8, 185-pound running back rushed for 155 yards and three touchdowns on nine carries in a 63-22 win over D.H. Conley. It was Pearson's third game in a row with 150 rushing yards or more.

Twenty-seven WASC swimmers combine for 57 first-place finishes in meet
